evidence.title: Waste management law
evidence.text: Waste management laws<section begin=overview /> govern the transport, treatment, storage, and disposal of all manner of waste, including municipal solid waste, hazardous waste, and nuclear waste, among many other types.

evidence.title: Waste management law
evidence.text: Waste laws are generally designed to minimize or eliminate the uncontrolled dispersal of waste materials into the environment in a manner that may cause ecological or biological harm, and include laws designed to reduce the generation of waste and promote or mandate waste recycling.

evidence.title: Waste management law
evidence.text: Regulatory efforts include identifying and categorizing waste types and mandating transport, treatment, storage, and disposal practices.

evidence.title: Waste management law
evidence.text: <section end=overview />

evidence.title: Composite liner
evidence.text: Disposing trash on Earth mainly comes in three ways: littering, incinerating, and storing in it the many landfills we have around the world.

evidence.title: Composite liner
evidence.text: With today’s landfills, there are very constructed contaminate structures.

evidence.title: Composite liner
evidence.text: These systems are designed to help keep solid waste from becoming too uncontained and uncontrolled from the environment and the impact it could have on the health of humans.

evidence.title: Composite liner
evidence.text: The purpose of having a liner system within a landfill is mainly to isolate everything within the landfill from the environment and protect it from contaminating the contents of the soil and especially the water within the ground.

evidence.title: Composite liner
evidence.text: These liners are engineered to create a physical barrier between the garbage within the landfill, the ground, and the environment, in order to separate the liquid contaminate (leachate) so that it can go to a treatment facility.

evidence.title: Composite liner
evidence.text: There are different types of these landfill sites for the different types of solid wastes which society creates and leaves behind.

evidence.title: Composite liner
evidence.text: There are certain levels of harmfulness in which the different types of trash have; therefore, there are different types of liner systems which are required for these different types of disposal sites.

evidence.title: Composite liner
evidence.text: The first type is single liner-systems.

evidence.title: Composite liner
evidence.text: These systems usually are put within landfills which mostly hold construction rubble.

evidence.title: Composite liner
evidence.text: These landfills are not meant to hold the disposal of harmful liquid wastes such as paint, tar, or any other type of liquid garbage that can easily seep through a single liner system.

evidence.title: Composite liner
evidence.text: The second type is double-liner systems.

evidence.title: Composite liner
evidence.text: These systems are usually found in municipal solid waste landfills as well all hazardous waste landfills.

evidence.title: Composite liner
evidence.text: The first part is constructed to collect the leachate while the second layer is engineered to be a leak-detection system to ensure that no contaminates leak into the ground and contaminate everything.

evidence.title: Household hazardous waste
evidence.text: Household hazardous waste (HHW), sometimes called retail hazardous waste or "home generated special materials', is post-consumer waste which qualifies as hazardous waste when discarded.

evidence.title: Household hazardous waste
evidence.text: It includes household chemicals and other substances for which the owner no longer has a use, such as consumer products sold for home care, personal care, automotive care, pest control and other purposes.

evidence.title: Household hazardous waste
evidence.text: These products exhibit many of the same dangerous characteristics as fully regulated hazardous waste due to their potential for reactivity, ignitability, corrosivity, toxicity, or persistence.

evidence.title: Household hazardous waste
evidence.text: Examples include drain cleaners, oil paint, motor oil, antifreeze, fuel, poisons, pesticides, herbicides and rodenticides, fluorescent lamps, lamp ballasts, smoke detectors, medical waste, some types of cleaning chemicals, and consumer electronics (such as televisions, computers, and cell phones).

evidence.title: Waste Land (film)
evidence.text: Waste Land is a 2010 British-Brazilian documentary film directed by Lucy Walker.

evidence.title: Waste Land (film)
evidence.text: The film chronicles artist Vik Muniz, who travels to the world's largest landfill, Jardim Gramacho outside Rio de Janeiro, to collaborate with a lively group of catadores of recyclable materials, who find a way to the most prestigious auction house in London via the surprising transformation of refuse into contemporary art.

evidence.title: Waste Land (film)
evidence.text: The catadores work in a co-operative founded and led by Sebastião Carlos Dos Santos, the ACAMJG, or Association of Pickers of Jardim Gramacho, who dreamed of improving life for his community.

evidence.title: Waste Land (film)
evidence.text: The money created by the selling of the artworks was given back to the catadores and the ACAMJG, as well as the prize money from the film awards, to help the catadores and their community.

evidence.title: Chemical waste
evidence.text: Chemical waste is a waste that is made from harmful chemicals (mostly produced by large factories).

evidence.title: Chemical waste
evidence.text: Chemical waste may fall under regulations such as COSHH in the United Kingdom, or the Clean Water Act and Resource Conservation and Recovery Act in the United States.

evidence.title: Chemical waste
evidence.text: In the U.S., the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA), as well as state and local regulations also regulate chemical use and disposal.

evidence.title: Chemical waste
evidence.text: Chemical waste may or may not be classed as hazardous waste.

evidence.title: Chemical waste
evidence.text: A chemical hazardous waste is a solid, liquid, or gaseous material that displays either a “Hazardous Characteristic” or is specifically “listed” by name as a hazardous waste.

evidence.title: Chemical waste
evidence.text: There are four characteristics chemical wastes may have to be considered as hazardous.

evidence.title: Chemical waste
evidence.text: These are Ignitability, Corrosivity, Reactivity, and Toxicity.

evidence.title: Chemical waste
evidence.text: This type of hazardous waste must be categorized as to its identity, constituents, and hazards so that it may be safely handled and managed.

evidence.title: Chemical waste
evidence.text: Chemical waste is a broad term and encompasses many types of materials.

evidence.title: Chemical waste
evidence.text: Consult the Material Safety Data Sheet (MSDS), Product Data Sheet or Label for a list of constituents.

evidence.title: Chemical waste
evidence.text: These sources should state whether this chemical waste is a waste that needs special disposal.

evidence.title: Business waste
evidence.text: Business (or commercial and industrial) waste – cover the commercial waste and industrial waste types .

evidence.title: Business waste
evidence.text: Generally, businesses are expected to make their own arrangements for the collection, treatment and disposal of their wastes.

evidence.title: Business waste
evidence.text: Waste from smaller shops and trading estates where local authority waste collection agreements are in place will generally be treated as municipal waste.

evidence.title: Shikashika
evidence.text: Shikashika is a shaved ice drink made from glacier ice in Peru and Bolivia.

evidence.title: Shikashika
evidence.text: In some rural communities, the extraction and sale of ice continues to be a primary natural resource for local economies.

evidence.title: Shikashika
evidence.text: Ice merchants extract the blocks with an axe by hand and transport them down from the mountains atop mules.

evidence.title: Shikashika
evidence.text: The unit of sale is usually an ice block weighing approximately 40 kilos which is sold to Shikashika vendors.

evidence.title: Shikashika
evidence.text: Each block sells for approximately 17 USD.

evidence.title: Shikashika
evidence.text: In turn, Shikashika is sold for approximately 15 cents in plastic bags with colorful sweet syrups at Andean festivals and on market day.

evidence.title: Shikashika
evidence.text: The word Shikashika is onomatopeia from the Amerindian language Quechua.

evidence.title: Shikashika
evidence.text: An alternative word for Shikashika in Spanish is "raspadilla."

evidence.title: Gerontion
evidence.text: "Gerontion" is a poem by T. S. Eliot that was first published in 1920.

evidence.title: Gerontion
evidence.text: The work relates the opinions and impressions of a gerontic, or elderly man, through a dramatic monologue which describes Europe after World War I through the eyes of a man who has lived the majority of his life in the 19th century.

evidence.title: Gerontion
evidence.text: Eliot considered using this already published poem as a preface to "The Waste Land", but decided to keep it as an independent poem.

evidence.title: Gerontion
evidence.text: Along with "The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock" and "The Waste Land", and other works published by Eliot in the early part of his career, '"Gerontion" discusses themes of religion, sexuality, and other general topics of modernist poetry.

evidence.title: Civic amenity site
evidence.text: A civic amenity site (CA site) or household waste recycling centre (HWRC) is a facility where the public can dispose of household waste and also often containing recycling points.

evidence.title: Civic amenity site
evidence.text: Civic amenity sites are run by the local authority in a given area.

evidence.title: Civic amenity site
evidence.text: Collection points for recyclable waste such as green waste, metals, glass and other waste types (including WVO) are available.

evidence.title: Civic amenity site
evidence.text: Items that cannot be collected by local waste collection schemes such as bulky waste are also provided.

evidence.title: Kulotunga Cinkaiariyan
evidence.text: Kulotunga Cinkaiariyan (Tamil: குலோத்துங்க சிங்கையாரியன் ) was the third of the Aryacakravarti kings of Jaffna Kingdom.

evidence.title: Kulotunga Cinkaiariyan
evidence.text: Author of the book “Ancient Jaffna” C. Rasanayagam calculated that he has been ruled Jaffna from 1256 to 1279 (23 years).

evidence.title: Kulotunga Cinkaiariyan
evidence.text: Yalpana Vaipava Malai says he followed his ancestor and promoted agriculture, and he converted waste land into agriculture land.

evidence.title: Kulotunga Cinkaiariyan
evidence.text: Also the book added that during his rule the kingdom was peaceful and prosper.
